q: What is the usual sequence for loading a concrete mixer?
n: Sand goes in first with part of the water so the cement does not stick to the drum; cement follows, then gravel, then the rest of the water to bring the batch to the right consistency. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate; DPWH Standard Specifications (Item 405, mixing).

q: What is Figure A that is a method of applying concrete or mortar pneumatically through a hose at high velocity onto a surface?
n: Shotcrete is mortar or concrete sprayed by compressed air through a hose at high velocity, so it compacts itself as it hits the surface. It is used for tunnels, slopes, pools and repairs. Source: ACI 506R, Guide to Shotcrete; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is Figure B that is a construction machine with rotating blades used to finish and smooth freshly poured concrete slabs?
n: A power trowel (helicopter) has motor-driven rotating steel blades that float and finish a large slab after the bleed water evaporates, giving a dense, smooth surface. Floats and screeds are hand or straightedge tools. Source: ACI 302.1R, Guide to Concrete Floor and Slab Construction.

q: What is Figure C that is a tool used to remove air pockets and ensure proper compaction of fresh concrete during placement?
n: An internal (poker) vibrator is dipped into fresh concrete to liquefy it briefly so trapped air rises out and the mix fills around bars and forms, preventing honeycombs. Source: ACI 309R, Guide for Consolidation of Concrete.

q: What is Figure D that is a type of concrete pump mounted on a truck with an articulated arm for placing concrete at heights or hard-to-reach areas?
n: A boom pump is mounted on a truck and carries the line on a folding (articulated) boom, so concrete can be placed directly at upper floors or far points. Trailer and line pumps push through hoses laid on the ground. Source: ACI 304.2R, Placing Concrete by Pumping Methods.

q: What is Figure E that is a type of connector used to resist shear forces between steel beams and concrete slabs in composite construction?
n: Headed shear studs are welded to the top flange of a steel beam and embedded in the slab, so beam and slab act together as one composite section and horizontal shear is transferred between them. Source: AISC 360 Chapter I (composite members); NSCP 2015 Chapter 5.

q: Which of these is a local maker of steel reinforcing bars?
n: SteelAsia Manufacturing Corporation is the country's largest maker of reinforcing bars, with mills in Bulacan, Cebu, Davao and Batangas. Source: SteelAsia company website (steelasia.com).

q: Which company supplies Portland cement in the Philippines?
n: Holcim Philippines produces portland and blended cements (Holcim Excel, Wallrite) in plants across the country. Mariwasa makes tiles and Puyat is known for steel and sports flooring. Source: Holcim Philippines company website.

q: What is the minimum rebar lap splice length allowed by code?
n: The NSCP (following ACI 318) sets tension lap splices at 1.0 or 1.3 times the development length, but never less than 300 mm. Source: NSCP 2015 Sec. 425.5 (lap splices); ACI 318-14 Sec. 25.5.

q: Beams under torsion need which stirrups?
n: Torsion produces diagonal tension that spirals around the member, so torsion reinforcement must be closed stirrups with 135° hooks, plus longitudinal bars at the corners. Open U-stirrups cannot resist it. Source: NSCP 2015 Sec. 409.7.6; ACI 318-14 Sec. 9.7.6.4.

q: What supports the rebars inside beam formwork at the right cover?
n: Bolsters and bar chairs are wire or plastic supports placed under the reinforcement so it sits at the required concrete cover above the form or subgrade. Source: CRSI Manual of Standard Practice; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is commonly used to protect column corners from impact?
n: Corner guards (metal, PVC or rubber angles) are fixed on exposed column and wall corners in corridors, parking areas and hospitals to absorb impacts from carts and vehicles. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What property does the slump test measure?
n: The slump test (ASTM C143) measures how far a cone of fresh concrete sags. It indicates consistency, the practical measure of workability, not water content or hardness. Source: ASTM C143; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: Which is NOT a component of concrete?
n: Concrete is cement, fine aggregate (sand), coarse aggregate (gravel) and water. Soil, clay and silt are contaminants that weaken the bond, which is why aggregates must be clean. Source: ASTM C33 (aggregates); DPWH Standard Specifications Item 405.

q: Which joint is sawn into concrete to create a planned line of weakness?
n: A contraction (control) joint is a groove sawn or tooled into the slab so shrinkage cracking happens along that planned line. Expansion (isolation) joints are full-depth gaps for movement. Source: ACI 224.3R, Joints in Concrete Construction.

q: Who is considered the father of prestressed concrete?
n: Eugène Freyssinet, a French engineer, developed and patented prestressed concrete with high-strength steel in 1928, and is called its father. Perret pioneered reinforced concrete architecture. Source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Eugène Freyssinet.

q: What is the correct sequence for removing formwork?
o: Columns, beam sides, beam soffit, slab soffit
Beam sides, columns, beam soffit, slab soffit
Slab soffit, columns, beam sides, beam soffit
Beam soffit, beam sides, columns, slab soffit
n: Forms that carry no load come off first: column sides, then beam sides, then the beam soffit and finally the slab soffit with its shores, once the concrete can carry its own weight. Source: ACI 347R, Guide to Formwork for Concrete; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: How soon can beam side forms be removed?
n: Beam side forms carry no load, so they can be stripped after about 1–2 days, once the concrete can hold its shape and is not damaged at the edges. Soffits and props stay much longer. Source: ACI 347R (formwork removal); DPWH Standard Specifications Item 903.

q: What must be ready when preparing formwork for a pour?
n: Before a pour, the formwork must be fully shored, braced and staged (scaffolding, props, walkways), so it carries the wet concrete and the workers safely. Materials are a separate concern. Source: ACI 347R, Guide to Formwork for Concrete; DOLE OSHS Rule 1414 (scaffolding).

q: How long do beam formwork and shores usually stay before removal?
n: Beam soffit forms and shores normally stay about 14 days (often up to 21 days for long spans) until the concrete reaches enough strength to carry its load. Source: ACI 347R (formwork removal); Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: How many 40 kg bags of cement are in one cubic meter of Class A concrete?
n: Fajardo's concrete proportion table gives 9.0 bags of 40 kg cement (or 7.0 bags of 50 kg) per cubic meter of Class A (1:2:4) concrete, with 0.50 m³ sand and 1.0 m³ gravel. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: Class A concrete is NOT the usual spec for which item?
n: Class A concrete is the structural mix for beams, girders, suspended slabs and slabs on fill. Pathwalks and other non-structural work use leaner Class C or D concrete. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate; DPWH Standard Specifications Item 405.

q: What is the standard mix proportion for Class A concrete?
n: Class A concrete is mixed 1 : 2 : 4 (cement : sand : gravel); AA is 1 : 1.5 : 3, B is 1 : 2.5 : 5 and C is 1 : 3 : 6. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: A 1:2:4 (Class A) concrete mix typically reaches about what compressive strength?
n: A 1 : 2 : 4 Class A mix is rated at about 3,500 psi (24 MPa) at 28 days in Fajardo's concrete classification. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: What is the most common use of Class A concrete in buildings?
n: Class A (1 : 2 : 4, about 3,500 psi) is the standard mix for structural members: beams, columns, girders and suspended slabs. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate; DPWH Standard Specifications Item 405.

q: How many truckloads of ready-mix concrete are needed for a 40 m × 50 m second-floor slab, 150 mm thick, if each truck carries 10 m³?
n: Volume = 40 × 50 × 0.15 = 300 m³. At 10 m³ per transit mixer, 300 ÷ 10 = 30 truckloads. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (volume method).

q: For a small residential project with a 40 sq.m. second-floor slab, which concrete method is most suitable?
n: A 40 m² slab at about 0.10–0.125 m thick is roughly 4–5 m³. That is too much to mix by hand and too little to justify ready-mix trucks, so a 2-bagger (two bags per batch) mixer is the practical choice. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (concreting methods).

q: What is the most practical method for pouring a 4 cu.m. concrete slab?
n: About 4 m³ is a small pour: ready-mix trucks carry 6–10 m³ with minimum-order charges, and hand mixing that much is slow and uneven. A 2-bagger mixer batches it efficiently on site. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (concreting methods).

q: What is the typical capacity of one transit mixer truck used for ready-mix concrete delivery in the Philippines?
n: Transit mixer trucks used by Philippine ready-mix suppliers typically carry 8–10 m³ per trip, and 10 m³ is the usual figure in quantity takeoffs. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate; ready-mix supplier specifications.

q: What should be considered first when choosing between ready-mix and site-mixed concrete?
n: The volume of concrete decides the method first: large volumes justify ready-mix trucks and pumps, while small volumes are site-mixed. Access, crew and schedule then refine the choice. Source: ACI 304R, Guide for Measuring, Mixing, Transporting and Placing Concrete.

q: How many 40 kg bags of cement go into 1 m³ of Class B concrete?
n: Fajardo's table gives 7.5 bags of 40 kg cement per m³ of Class B (1 : 2.5 : 5) concrete (6.0 bags of 50 kg). Since 7.5 is not among 7, 9 or 10, the answer is "none of the above". Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: A 1 : 2.5 : 5 mix is classified as:
n: A 1 : 2.5 : 5 (cement : sand : gravel) mix is Class B. Class A is 1 : 2 : 4 and Class C is 1 : 3 : 6. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: What is the typical compressive strength of Class B concrete?
n: Class B (1 : 2.5 : 5) concrete is rated at about 3,000 psi (21 MPa) at 28 days in Fajardo's classification, a step below Class A at 3,500 psi. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: A 1 : 3 : 6 mix is classified as:
n: A 1 : 3 : 6 mix is Class C, a lean mix for non-structural work. Class D is 1 : 3.5 : 7. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: Class B concrete is commonly used for:
n: Class B concrete suits lightly stressed elements such as footings, slabs on fill and walls on grade. Beams, columns and suspended slabs need Class A. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate; DPWH Standard Specifications Item 405.
